items.prompt: Why does "any feedback?" tend to produce vague answers like "looks good," even from people who genuinely have real opinions?
choices: Because people are usually dishonest when asked for feedback

A vague, open-ended question makes a vague answer the easiest, lowest-risk response available — it's not that there's nothing to say, it's that the question doesn't require anything specific to be said
Because "looks good" is always factually false in these situations
Because most people don't actually read what they're asked to review
items.explanation: The vague default isn't necessarily dishonesty — it's the natural equilibrium of a question with no specific target. A vague answer to a vague question costs no effort and carries no social risk, which is exactly what a narrower question closes off.

items.prompt: Per L2, why does asking "how was the tradeoffs section?" tend to produce more useful feedback than "any feedback on this doc?"
choices: Because it's a shorter question and shorter questions are always answered more carefully

Because a specific question closes off the easy vague-answer exit — plausibly answering it with "looks good" would itself read as having skipped the section, making a real answer the new path of least resistance
Because tradeoffs sections are inherently more interesting than other parts of a document
There's no real difference; question phrasing doesn't affect answer quality
items.explanation: The mechanism is about what counts as an easy, low-risk answer. A specific question makes a generic response implausible as a complete answer, which pushes the respondent toward giving genuinely specific, useful feedback instead.

items.prompt: In L3's Request 3, why does asking "did you read the whole doc or mainly the tradeoffs section?" matter, given the reviewer already gave a specific, useful comment?
choices: It doesn't matter — one good comment proves the whole doc was read carefully

It calibrates how much confidence to place in the REST of the doc — the specific tradeoffs comment shows that section was read carefully, but says nothing about whether the rest was reviewed with the same attention
It's only useful for checking whether the reviewer is being honest
It's unnecessary because all feedback should be weighted equally regardless of engagement level
items.explanation: Calibration is a separate skill from getting a specific answer — knowing that the tradeoffs feedback was high-signal doesn't tell you anything about the parts that weren't asked about, which is exactly what the follow-up question in L3 was designed to surface.

items.prompt: Per L2, if someone doesn't believe candid criticism is welcome, will a well-phrased, specific question reliably produce useful feedback from them?
choices: Yes — question phrasing alone always overrides any concerns about how feedback will be received

Not reliably — psychological safety is a precondition alongside good question phrasing; a specific question can still get a safe, vague answer if the person doesn't trust that candor is genuinely welcome
No, phrasing has no effect on feedback quality whatsoever, only trust does
Yes, but only if the question is asked in writing rather than verbally
items.explanation: L2 frames these as two parts that work together, not substitutes for each other — a better-shaped question increases the chance of a real answer, but it doesn't override a well-founded fear that candor will be held against the person giving it.

items.prompt: Per L3's failure modes, what's the difference between a good calibration follow-up and a defensive, safety-eroding one?
choices: There's no real difference — any follow-up question after feedback reads the same way to the recipient

A good follow-up is framed around the asker's own next steps ("I want to know if I should expect gaps elsewhere"); a defensive one implies the reviewer should have done more ("you should have read the whole thing"), which discourages honest engagement next time
Follow-up questions should never be asked, regardless of framing
The difference is purely about question length, not framing
items.explanation: L3 explicitly distinguishes the two: the same literal question can either extend the safety that produced an honest answer, or undermine it, depending on whether it's framed as the asker's own information need or as an audit of the reviewer's effort.

items.prompt: Per L3's second failure mode, is "only ask for feedback once something is finished" always the right scoping rule?
choices: Yes, always — feedback on unfinished work is never useful

No — while scoping to something specific and finished worked well for the doc-review scenario, over-applying that as "only ask when complete" wastes the chance to catch a bad direction early; the real principle is "specific and answerable," not always "complete"
Yes, because unfinished work cannot be scoped specifically
No, because feedback should never be scoped to specific sections at all
items.explanation: L3 explicitly warns against over-generalizing the 'specific and finished' example into an absolute rule — the actual transferable principle is asking something specific and answerable, which can apply to an early direction check just as well as a finished draft.
